You can push a prod deploy on a Friday afternoon, but only with approval from the on-call engineering manager. Friday deploys aren't in the normal window, which is Monday through Thursday, 09:00–16:00 Pacific [1].

Today is the last business day of October, so the month-end billing freeze applies to Ledger. No normal changes to Ledger are allowed from the last business day of the month until invoices are sent, usually on the 2nd [2]. If your deploy touches Ledger, it's blocked today regardless of approval.

Other points:
- **Normal changes** (such as schema migrations, infrastructure config, or auth and billing logic) also need sign-off from the owning team's change approver. Changes to Restricted services need Security sign-off too [2][3].
- **Canary:** every deploy goes to a 5% canary cell first and is promoted automatically after 20 minutes if error rates and p95 latency stay within 10% of baseline [1].
- **Rollbacks** are always allowed, at any time, without approval, including during freezes [1][2].

The nightly hotel limit for London is **$350**. The expense and travel policy sets hotels at up to $250 per night in most cities, and $350 in New York, San Francisco, London and Tokyo [1].

Book the hotel through Navan so the company can find you in an emergency [1]. Expenses go in Ramp within 30 days, with an itemized receipt for anything over $25 [1].

Patients with household income **under 250% of the federal poverty level** qualify for the sliding-fee program. It reduces visit costs by **40–100%** [1]. The source gives that range but doesn't say which income levels get which percentage, so I can't tell you where a given patient falls within it.

Some other points that may help:

- **Self-pay rates before any discount:** new patient $165, established patient $120, telehealth $79, annual physical $195 [1].
- **Prompt-pay discount:** self-pay patients who pay in full at the time of service get 20% off [1]. The source doesn't say whether this stacks with the sliding-fee reduction.
- **Applying:** front desk staff can start the application at check-in [1].
- **Payment plans:** if a balance is still owed, plans of up to 12 months with no interest are available for balances over $200 [1].
- **No denial of care:** no patient is denied care for inability to pay [1].

Critical results must reach the ordering clinician within 60 minutes. If that clinician can't be reached within 30 minutes, the result goes to the medical director on call [1]. Each notification is documented in the chart with the time and the person notified [1].

A related rule covers critical values called in by the reference lab: the supervising physician must be notified within 30 minutes [1]. The protocol doesn't say how this fits with the 60-minute rule, so confirm with your clinical lead which applies to your situation.

A customer who prepays Growth annually saves **15%**, which is **$2,160 per year** [1]. The Growth list price is $1,200/month, or $14,400/year, so the prepaid price is $12,240 per year [1].

The policy also says multi-year deals can add an extra 5% per committed year, capped at 10%, on top of the first-year discount. That extra does not count toward the discount approval thresholds [1].

Visit links expire **2 hours after the scheduled end time** [1]. The October 2026 Juniper steering committee confirmed the same rule [2].

This rule is in the requirements for the new telehealth platform, which is still being rolled out. Halcyon's current platform is Larkspur Telehealth, and the knowledge base doesn't say how long its links stay active after a visit [5].

Emergency workspace access lasts **2 hours**. A second engineer from the support or on-call rotation must approve it [1].

**Approval:**
- Run `nwctl access request --workspace <id> --reason <case-or-incident-id>` [1].
- A second engineer approves in Teleport. You can't approve your own request, and the approver can't be on the same case [1].
- The request must reference an open support case or a declared incident. Curiosity or speed alone doesn't qualify [1].

**Limits:**
- Access is read-only by default. Write access, such as editing a pipeline on the customer's behalf, needs the customer's written consent recorded in the case first [1].
- If you need more time, submit a new request with an update on the case [1].
- Standard production sessions last 8 hours, so the emergency window is deliberately shorter [1][2].

All sessions are recorded, and customer-data access must be tied to a support case or incident ticket [2].

The Patient Safety Committee is chaired by the Chief Medical Officer, Dr. Kenji Watanabe [1][2]. The committee reviews sentinel events and completed root cause analyses with their action plans, meets monthly, and tracks every action item to closure [2].

No. Removing the name doesn't make a patient's history safe to paste into a chatbot at Halcyon Health.

- **Removing the name is not enough.** The approved AI tools list says "de-identified" is not a loophole, and you should treat any patient details as protected health information (PHI) [1].
- **Public chatbots are not approved.** The list explicitly bars public chatbots and general-purpose AI assistants on any device, including personal phones [1]. The HIPAA policy also says never to put PHI into AI tools that are not on the approved list [3].
- **Halcyon Assist is not an exception.** It is the internal assistant, but it is for policy questions only. Do not paste patient details into it, even without names [1].

**What you can use for patient summaries:**
- **Quillon Ambient** is approved for PHI, but only at the Riverside and Elm Park pilot clinics. It requires patient verbal consent at the start of each visit, and a clinician must review and sign every note [1][2].
- **Meridian draft replies** are approved for PHI inside Meridian EHR. A clinician must edit or approve each draft before it is sent [1].
- **Meridian EHR** holds the full clinical record, so the summary should come from there [4].

If you think a chatbot tool would help your work, contact the Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) and the HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui). A new tool needs a security risk assessment, a signed business associate agreement, an inventory entry, and, for clinical use, a clinical safety review by the CMIO. Turnaround is typically 6–10 weeks [1].

rows.answer: The legacy `/v1/track` ingest endpoint will stop accepting events on **April 30, 2027**, according to the Northwind Pipelines changelog [1]. The same entry notes that SDKs released after March 2025 already use `/v2/events` [1].

**287 workspaces** had duplicate invoices in the October incident (INC-2340), and **$184,300** was refunded [1].

- **Duplicate invoices:** 312 across 287 workspaces. Card customers on auto-pay were affected, and 201 of those invoices were auto-charged [1].
- **Refunds:** All 201 auto-charges were refunded, totaling $184,300. The other 111 invoices were voided rather than refunded [1].

The source doesn't say how many workspaces received a refund. The 201 charges may not map one-to-one to the 287 workspaces, so I can't give a refunded-workspace count from these documents.

**17 lab results** from Bayline Reference Laboratories were filed into the wrong patient's charts at the Riverside and Northgate clinics between July 21 and 23, 2026 [1]. The incident was classified as a Level 2 adverse event. Two patients had follow-up on abnormal results delayed by four and six days, and neither suffered lasting harm [1].

The root cause analysis identified three main causes [1]:

- **A silent format change by Bayline.** On July 20, Bayline changed its results feed and moved the medical record number (MRN) into a different HL7 segment, without notice [1].
- **Weak fallback matching at Halcyon.** When the MRN was missing, the interface engine (Switchyard) matched results on last name and year of birth only. That rule had existed since 2021 and had never been used at volume [1].
- **No monitoring and no contractual notice requirement.** Nobody was alerted that 100% of Bayline results were using the fallback rule, and the Bayline agreement did not require advance notice of feed changes [1].

The problem was caught on July 23, when a medical assistant at Riverside noticed a potassium result that did not match the patient's history. All 17 results were moved to the correct charts by July 24 [1].

Corrective actions [1]:

- Removing the name-and-birth-year fallback, with unmatched results sent to a manual queue (done, Sept 15).
- An alert when more than 1% of any lab's results use a fallback match in an hour (done, Sept 30).
- Amending the lab agreement to require 30 days' notice of feed changes (in progress, due Dec 31).
- Adding a positive patient identification check before results are released to the patient portal (in progress, due Nov 30).
cited_titles: Root cause analysis: lab results filed to the wrong patient chart (RCA-26-07)

Halcyon doesn't have a direct equivalent to a five-business-day postmortem deadline. Its closest rule is a **45-calendar-day** deadline to complete a root cause analysis (RCA) for Level 1 and Level 2 events, counted from when the event becomes known [1].

The relevant timeline for a sentinel (Level 1) event, which includes severe temporary harm and wrong-patient procedures [1]:

| When | What | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Immediately | Make the patient safe and tell the charge nurse on shift | [1] |
| Within 1 hour | Charge nurse notifies the on-call medical director | [1] |
| Immediately | Anyone involved or who witnessed the event files a SafeReport | [1] |
| Within 72 hours | Quality & Patient Safety (QPS) charters the RCA team | [1] |
| Within 45 calendar days | RCA is completed, with its action plan | [1] |

The policy also requires the attending clinician to disclose the event to the patient or family [1]. Completed RCAs go to the Patient Safety Committee, chaired by Chief Medical Officer Dr. Kenji Watanabe, which meets monthly [1].

For example, an RCA for lab results filed to the wrong chart (events July 21–23, 2026) was completed August 28, 2026, within that 45-day window [2].

The Halcyon Health documents don't use the term "incident commander" for clinic patient events. For a patient safety event at a clinic, the **charge nurse on shift** coordinates the immediate response. If the clinic has no charge nurse on shift, the clinic manager takes that role [1]. The charge nurse assigns who stays with the patient, who calls the family, and who secures equipment, medications or records involved [1].

For a sentinel event, the charge nurse must notify the on-call medical director within 1 hour [1]. The attending clinician discloses the event to the patient or family, with the charge nurse or medical director present [1]. The clinical escalation protocol covers the first clinical steps, such as calling 911 and notifying the on-site clinician [2].

The "incident commander" role that appears in the knowledge base belongs to Northwind Labs, a separate organization. It is the engineering on-call role that runs software incidents, not clinic patient events [8][9].

Halcyon Health gives more fixed leave than Northwind Labs, at least on the minimums the documents state.

- **Halcyon Health:** Annual leave is 20 days a year in years 1–3 and 25 days from year 4 [2]. Staff get 9 paid holidays, and up to 56 hours can carry over into the next year [2]. The October 2026 policy replaces the older PTO rules, which had 8 holidays and a 40-hour carry-over [1][2].
- **Northwind Labs:** Leave is flexible PTO with a minimum of 15 days a year that staff are expected to actually take [6]. The sources I found don't mention a holiday count or carry-over rules for Northwind.

On the headline numbers, Halcyon's guaranteed minimum is 20 days in years 1–3, which is 5 days more than Northwind's 15-day minimum. Halcyon also has a fixed 25 days from year 4. Northwind's flexible model may still offer more in practice, but the documents don't say so. The Northwind welcome guide I found is undated, so it may not reflect current terms. If you need the full Northwind picture, check with its People team.

Halcyon needs a **signed business associate agreement (BAA)** before any patient data goes to a vendor, and a **security risk assessment** should be completed. The documents use "BAA" rather than "DPA," so I did not find a separate DPA requirement.

**Required before any PHI is disclosed**
- **Signed BAA.** A vendor that will create, receive, maintain or transmit PHI on Halcyon's behalf is a business associate, and a signed BAA is required before any PHI is disclosed. This includes test files or "just a few names" for a pilot [1].
- **Security risk assessment.** Systems and vendors handling PHI need one [4][2]. Halcyon's own examples show the assessment is done before go-live or contract execution, e.g., Quillon's was completed in July 2026 [3].

**Also required for new systems**
- An entry in the clinical and business systems inventory before go-live. The HIPAA Security Officer maintains this list [4].
- For clinical AI tools, a clinical safety review by the CMIO [2].
- Contact the Privacy Officer (Margaret Holloway) and the HIPAA Security Officer (Ahmed Siddiqui) [2][4].

**Current example:** Tallgrass Survey Co. passed its security risk assessment in September 2026, but its BAA is still unexecuted, so no PHI may be shared with it yet [1]. Halcyon's approved AI tool guidance also says removing a name does not make data non-identifiable, so treat patient details as PHI [2].

Yes, Northwind has an equivalent, but it covers customer workspaces, not patient records. Northwind doesn't handle EHR data, so the two are built for different risks.

**Northwind:** "Emergency access to customer workspaces" lets support, solutions and on-call engineers look inside a customer's workspace when an open support case or declared incident requires it [2]. The main differences from Halcyon's process:

| | Halcyon Health (EHR break-the-glass) | Northwind Labs (emergency workspace access) |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | Urgent clinical need to open a chart outside the user's normal patient panel [1] | An open support case or declared incident; every request must cite the case or incident ID [2] |
| Approval | None in the moment; the user picks a reason and types a justification [1] | A second engineer from support or on-call must approve in Teleport, and cannot be on the same case [2] |
| Duration | Up to 12 hours, until end of shift [1] | 2 hours, shorter than the standard 8-hour production session [2][4] |
| Default access | Full chart access for the session | Read-only; write access needs the customer's written consent in the case [2] |
| Review | Every event logged and reviewed by the Privacy Officer's team within 2 business days; manager confirms unclear reasons [1] | Sessions recorded and kept one year; the customer's audit log shows the access and enterprise admins are emailed within 24 hours; security samples sessions weekly and reviews every write session [2] |
| Misuse | Treated as a privacy incident, with sanctions up to termination [1] | Prohibited uses include accessing a workspace belonging to someone you know personally [2] |

**Key difference:** Halcyon's design prioritizes speed for patient care, so it has no pre-approval and relies on after-the-fact review. Northwind requires a second engineer to approve before access starts, keeps access read-only by default, and uses a shorter window. Northwind also notifies the customer, which Halcyon's process does not mention.

Halcyon's general HIPAA policy also suspends clinical system access if HIPAA training is more than 14 days overdue, and reviews EHR access logs monthly [3]. Northwind's broader access rules, such as Teleport-based production access and quarterly access reviews, are in its information security policy [4].
cited_titles: HIPAA privacy and PHI handling policy

**Halcyon Health: no.** Slack is never allowed for PHI, including DMs [1]. Its HIPAA policy also says PHI may never go in Slack, and it may only be stored in the EHR, the practice management system, and approved systems on the intranet [3]. For patient communication, use the EHR's secure messaging, or `[secure]` encrypted email for outside providers [3].

**Northwind Labs: it depends on the data class.**
- **Restricted** data (customer event payloads, credentials, encryption keys) never goes in Slack or tickets [2]. The emergency-access policy repeats this: use field names and counts instead of pasting payloads [4].
- **Confidential** data (financials, contracts, employee data) is shared on a need-to-know basis [2]. The sources I found don't explicitly ban Slack for this class, so check with the owning team if you're unsure.
- **Internal** and **Public** data have no Slack restrictions beyond normal sharing [2].
- Northwind's policy allows exceptions only with written approval from the Head of Security, and they expire after 90 days [2]. I found no exception process for Halcyon's Slack rule.

Report suspected incidents or accidental exposure in `#security-help` [2][4]. Northwind's policy says good-faith reports are never penalized [2].

You need two sign-offs, plus an ADR if the change alters how long data is kept.

1. **Platform change approver (PLAT):** Oluwaseun Adeyemi, with Kofi Mensah as delegate. Driftwood, the archive where these events live, is owned by PLAT [7][5]. Lifecycle rules on Driftwood buckets are a normal change, which requires the owning team's change approver [1][2].
2. **Head of Security or security on-call:** Driftwood stores Restricted data, so normal changes to it also need Tomasz Wierzbicki (Head of Security) or the security on-call delegate [1][7][5].

Other requirements:

- **ADR:** Any change that alters how long customer data is kept needs an ADR, linked from the PR [1].
- **Customer notice:** Shortening retention needs 30 days' notice from the account team for Enterprise contracts that reference a retention period [1].
- **PR process:** Add the `change:normal` label, fill in the risk and rollback sections, and request the approver as a CODEOWNERS reviewer. Add `@northwind/security` for Restricted services. Approvals expire after 7 days [1].
- **Freezes:** Normal changes are blocked from December 18, 2026 to January 4, 2027, and from the last business day of each month until invoices go out (usually the 2nd). Rollbacks are always allowed [1].

If you're proposing a retention change, the current default is 365 days for archived event payloads under the v2 standard, effective September 15, 2026 [2]. The security team owns that standard, and extending archive retention beyond it for an Enterprise customer needs its approval [2][3].

The sign-off came from the **Head of Security**, who approved security exception **SEC-EX-117** on August 24, 2026. The exception covers the Hollowpine helpdesk (VEN-031) while its DPA remains unsigned [1]. The register names the role, not an individual.

**How long it lasts:** Under the information security policy, exceptions require written approval from the Head of Security and expire after 90 days [5]. Counting 90 days from August 24 puts expiry around **November 22, 2026**, about three weeks from today. That date is my calculation, not one stated in the documents.

**What happens at expiry:** If the DPA is still unsigned, Support Operations must either get the exception renewed or move ticket intake back to email [1].

**Other conditions:**
- The security review passed only conditionally. AI reply suggestions must stay disabled until the DPA is signed [1].
- The main open DPA point is Hollowpine's right to use ticket content to train its reply-suggestion model. Redlines have been with legal since August [1].
- The contract renews January 31, 2027 [1].

Changing the send time is a **significant change**, so it needs three approvals:

1. **System steward: Felix Brandt.** Pillbox, the medication reminder scheduler, is owned by Digital Health Engineering, Patient Engagement (DHE-PE), and Brandt is that team's steward [2][3].
2. **Clinical safety sign-off: Dr. Anjali Rao, CMIO**, or her delegate, Associate CMIO Dr. Benedict Osei [2].
3. **Review at the weekly Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB)**, which meets Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [2].

The policy lists patient-facing automation such as reminders as a significant change [2]. It also says that any scheduler change, including moving a job to a new runner, requires a written runbook that states how double-sending is prevented. That rule came from the September 2026 incident where duplicate reminders went out [1][2].

The fix would need three approvals, because it changes how results are routed:

1. **System steward, Owen Mbeki (Integration Services).** He approves changes to the interface engine, Switchyard, which is owned by the INT team [2][7].
2. **Clinical safety sign-off from the CMIO, Dr. Anjali Rao**, or her delegate, Associate CMIO Dr. Benedict Osei [2].
3. **Review at the weekly Clinical Systems Change Advisory Board (CSCAB)**, which meets Wednesdays at 14:00 Eastern [2].

The change-control policy classes any change to "medication information, orders or results routing" as significant, and the root cause analysis says changes to result routing fall under that rule [2][1]. The emergency path, where the on-call medical director can approve, applies only to stopping ongoing patient harm, and the feed was already stopped and restored by July 24 [2][1].

Some of the RCA's corrective actions were already marked done, including removing the name-and-birth-year fallback matching (due Sept 15) and the alert for fallback matches (due Sept 30) [1]. The positive patient identification check, owned by Clinical Informatics (steward Grace Oyelaran), was still in progress with a Nov 30 due date [1][2]. The knowledge base doesn't say whether the completed fixes went through this approval path, so I can't confirm that from the documents.

The cycle scope covers CDC-backed snapshots, the editor preview, dead-letter routing for unmatched events, and a private beta with design partners in October. The GA target stays January 2027 [1]. 2. **Lantern: self-serve billing portal.** Pitched by NH and HV. The original target was beta in December and GA in January 2027, and it depends on the payment-provider migration finishing first [1]. Since then, GA has slipped to March 2027 and beta has moved to February, because the migration won't finish until mid-January and INC-2340 showed the need for an invoice-history view [3].

3. **Hydrant: automatic scaling for ingest gateways per cell.** Pitched by OA. It includes the gateway TLS session ticket change from INC-2291 as a small batch item [1]. The October offsite notes say Hydrant is on track for the end of cycle 5 [3].

**Mostly yes, though the evidence for one item is indirect.** The postmortem lists four action items. Three are marked done, and a September changelog entry confirms the fourth.

Archived customer event data is kept for **365 days** by default. This is set in the current retention standard (v2), effective September 15, 2026, which replaced the earlier 400-day default [2].

- **Hot buffer (Kafka):** event payloads are kept for 7 days before archiving [2].
- **Archive (Driftwood):** payloads are kept for 365 days. Object-storage lifecycle rules delete them once they pass the period, and per-workspace overrides are stored as bucket tags [2].
- **Enterprise contracts:** customers can contract for a shorter archive period [1]. They can also contract for longer retention, up to 730 days, with security team approval [2].

The Pricing and discount policy still refers to a 400-day limit for custom retention, which matches the older v1 standard, not v2 [4]. Treat that policy as possibly out of date.

Northwind Labs has **14 days** to complete deletion of a verified GDPR request in all live systems. This comes from the Customer data retention standard v2, effective September 15, 2026, which replaced the older 30-day requirement [1]. The 14-day clock runs from the verified request [1].

- **Live systems:** deleted within 14 days [1].
- **Backups:** not deleted on that timeline. They age out on the normal 35-day schedule [1].
- **Internal alert:** support logs every request in the `data-requests` queue, which alerts at day 10 [1].

Primary on-call will pay **$500 per week**, plus **$150 per page outside business hours**. Mid-November shifts fall under the new rates, which take effect for shifts starting on or after Tuesday, November 3, 2026 [1].

The increase replaces the older runbook figures of $400 per week and $100 per page [1][2]. The new memo also adds a **$1,500 per week cap on out-of-hours page pay**, which is not in the runbook [1]. The October offsite notes confirm the on-call pay increase was approved [3].

You can roll over up to **56 hours** of unused annual leave into the next calendar year [1]. The annual leave policy took effect October 1, 2026, and replaces the old PTO rule, which allowed 40 hours [1][2]. The first carry-over under the new limit happens on January 1, 2027 [1].

Hours above the limit are paid out in January at your current rate [1]. Full-time staff accrue 6.15 hours per pay period in years 1–3 and 7.7 hours from year 4 [1].

An Enterprise customer can use reference tables of up to **500 million rows per workspace**, according to the streaming joins product spec [1]. The Growth plan limit is 50 million rows [1].

This is a spec-level target, not a confirmed product limit. The same spec lists the feature as approved for the Q4 cycle [1]. Tributary is in private beta, with GA targeted for January 2027 [3].

The 500 million figure is also not yet backed by the snapshot design. RFC-031 describes a 50M-row table as the reference point, noting that a restart rebuild takes about 25 minutes [2]. The RFC proposes persisting snapshots to make restores under 90 seconds for a 50M-row table [2]. It also keeps a 2 GiB per-partition memory budget for reference state, with partitions spilling to disk when they exceed it [2]. Its approval was still pending a threat-model sign-off when that document was written [2].

The new telehealth platform, Juniper, is scheduled to reach patients in two phases, starting with a pilot on **January 12, 2027** at Riverside, Elm Park and Northgate clinics. The network-wide launch is **March 2, 2027**, covering all clinics and the telehealth front desk [1].

- **Go/no-go for the pilot:** December 16, 2026. The criteria are join success above 98% for two consecutive weeks, zero open Level 1–2 safety findings, and CSCAB approval as a significant change [1].
- **Current status:** Internal testing showed 98.7% join success across 1,900 test visits, against a goal of above 98% [1].
- **Larkspur shutdown:** The current vendor, Larkspur Telehealth, is not being renewed past December 31, 2026. A month-to-month extension runs through March 31, 2027 [3][1].

The dates come from the October 21, 2026 steering committee notes, so they are a plan that depends on the December 16 decision [1].

No, the knowledge base has no record of Tomasz Wierzbicki (Head of Security) signing off on LZ's RFC-031. The most recent records show it still pending.

- **RFC status:** The RFC's approval table lists TW (Security) as "Pending." TW wants a threat model for copying Restricted data across tiers before approving, and nothing ships to the private beta until TW signs off [1].
- **October status:** At the October leadership offsite, Dmitri noted that security sign-off on persisted snapshots was still outstanding and was the main risk to Tomasz's timeline for Tributary [3].
- **Action item:** Dmitri was tasked with unblocking the RFC-031 security review with Tomasz by the end of October [3]. Today is October 30, so that deadline is now.

The latest document I found is from early October, so a sign-off after that may not be recorded here. Check with Tomasz or Dmitri to confirm the current status.

The self-serve billing portal (internally called **Lantern**) is now expected to reach general availability in **March 2027**, up from January 2027. The slip was decided at the October 2026 leadership offsite. The payment-provider migration won't finish until mid-January, and the team needs the invoice-history view to handle voided invoices properly after INC-2340 [2].

- **Original plan:** beta in December 2026, GA in January 2027 [1].
- **Current plan:** beta in February 2027, GA in March 2027 [2].

I found no source dated after the October 1 offsite notes, so this may have changed since then.

The only related reference is from the October 2026 leadership offsite. Joanne Pryce presented parental leave benchmarking, but the decision was deferred to the December meeting, and the notes say there is "no change to the current policy yet" [1]. The current policy itself isn't in the sources.

For the actual figure, check with the People team (Joanne Pryce is VP People, per the offsite notes [1]) or ask in `#ask-anything`, which the onboarding guide says People monitors during business hours [2].

The only related detail is from the root cause analysis of the July 2026 misfiling event. It says the "Bayline agreement" does not require advance notice of feed format changes, and it lists an action to amend the "lab services agreement" to require 30 days' notice. That amendment is owned by Lab contracts and Clinical Operations, due December 31, and marked in progress [1]. That is an amendment, not a renewal date.

To find the renewal date, check with Lab contracts or Clinical Operations, or confirm whether the Bayline agreement is a lab services contract that has its own BAA record.
